children: Donald Trump will gladly pay Americans $5,000 each next year for their votes in November. The U.S. president's latest giveaway, unveiled at a Republican gathering on Wednesday, lacks the $1 trillion of funding or any clear economic rationale. It befits the administration’s slapdash approach, but also exacerbates clashing agendas at the White House, Treasury Department and Federal Reserve in a murky Bermuda Triangle of policy that is increasingly unnerving investors.

This week’s tumult epitomizes the relentless unpredictability. Trump escalated his trade fracas with Canada, eroding bilateral investment between neighbors and raising costs for vital industries such as auto manufacturing and agriculture. The unprompted war with Iran further spiraled into broader regional conflict, with new Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and U.S. bombing of Iranian oil tankers, which sent crude prices past $100 a barrel. A $6 billion buyback of Treasury bonds expanded the agency's vexing market intervention in the market.

Moreover, the country's budget deficit is set to exceed $2 trillion this fiscal year, with federal debt surpassing the ignominious $40 trillion mark and 100% of GDP milestones. With plenty of high-grade corporate debt to buy, bond investors have been selling off Treasury bills, pushing 10-year yields beyond 4.8%. The producer price index, a measure of wholesale inflation before it reaches consumers, also has jumped sharply, with economists forecasting worse to come as costs for inputs, including diesel, stay high.

The only unifying theme among these quandaries is that they are all at least partly self-inflicted. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's reactive bond buying muzzles the intended signals, with quickly rebounding yields eating away at his credibility. Trump’s fiscally dangerous new pledge to send out checks if his party retains congressional power after November's midterm elections evokes earlier empty promises. Where are the payouts from Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency savings or the commander-in-chief's highly touted tariff dividends?

This inscrutable mess probably leaves Fed Chair Kevin Warsh to try and steady the ship by raising interest rates. It would be an imperfect and incomplete step that also defies Trump's avowed desire for lower borrowing costs. It would be no mystery at all, however, if the economic vortex makes markets' faith disappear.
Follow Gabriel Rubin on Bluesky and LinkedIn.

President Donald Trump on September 9 proposed to pay every U.S. adult a $5,000 "Trump dividend" if ​Republicans keep control of Congress in the November midterm elections. The pledge came during the first day of a party convention being held in Dallas.

The Treasury Department said on the same day that it would ‌repurchase as much as $6 billion in 10- to 20-year U.S. ​bonds during a buyback ​operation on September 10, triple ⁠the amount of its ​last such operation.
